packet.headline_seed: Sacked Ukrainian defence minister calls for presidential election
packet.description_seed: Martial law has been in place in Ukraine since February 2022, under which elections are suspended.

what: Sacked Ukrainian defence minister calls for presidential election

clean_source_blocks.text: Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for wartime elections, in what many see as the biggest challenge to Volodymyr Zelensky's presidency since war broke out with Russia in February 2022. "Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia," said Fedorov, 35, in a video posted to YouTube on Tuesday, adding that Ukraine is fighting "precisely because we want to remain a free European state". Since Russia's invasion Ukraine has been under martial law, which means elections are suspended. Fedorov, who did not mention Zelensky by name in the video, was unexpectedly fired from his role as defence minister in late July, just six months after his appointment. Zelensky is yet to respond to the video from Fedorov, whose dismissal sparked protests across the country.
Martial law has been in place in Ukraine since February 2022, under which elections are suspended.

During his tenure as defence minister, Fedorov was credited with energising the ministry, heading a drive against corruption and using data to analyse and try to improve performance on the front line. His dismissal is widely accepted to have been related to tensions between him and army commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi. Syrskyi was also replaced several weeks later, after weeks of protests piled pressure onto the Ukrainian president. Fedorov gave no indication as to his own political plans in the YouTube video, instead focusing on the need for a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amidst a prolonged war".

Mr Zelensky has repeatedly rejected the notion of holding elections during wartime, despite demands from Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, as well as some factions of Ukrainian society. Protesters took to the streets of Kyiv after the sacking of Mykhailo Fedorov - Reuters Mr Fedorov's address came hours after Mr Zelensky announced that he would formally nominate Maj Gen Yevhen Khmara, a former security service (SBU) official, to take over the defence ministry. His comments amounted to one of the most significant challenges to the Ukrainian president since the start of the war. The former defence minister's trust rating soared from 35 per cent to 65 per cent after he was ousted in July, surpassing that of Mr Zelensky. In a poll published by the Rating Group that month, 72 per cent of respondents said they opposed his dismissal.

Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for wartime elections, in what many see as the biggest challenge to Volodymyr Zelensky's presidency since war broke out with Russia in February 2022.

"Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia," said Fedorov, 35, in a video posted to YouTube on Tuesday, adding that Ukraine is fighting "precisely because we want to remain a free European state".

Since Russia's invasion Ukraine has been under martial law, which means elections are suspended.

Fedorov, who did not mention Zelensky by name in the video, was unexpectedly fired from his role as defence minister in late July, just six months after his appointment.

Zelensky is yet to respond to the video from Fedorov, whose dismissal sparked protests across the country.

During his tenure as defence minister, Fedorov was credited with energising the ministry, heading a drive against corruption and using data to analyse and try to improve performance on the front line.

His dismissal is widely accepted to have been related to tensions between him and army commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi. Syrskyi was also replaced several weeks later, after weeks of protests piled pressure onto the Ukrainian president.

Fedorov gave no indication as to his own political plans in the YouTube video, instead focusing on the need for a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amidst a prolonged war".

He added that the country was facing a "systemic crisis of governance" and is "scared of change", and pointed to corruption in Ukraine as one of the things hurting the country's war effort.

Zelensky has since appointed Yevgeniy Khmara, a career intelligence official with a low political profile, as acting defence minister.

Other posts in Zelensky's government were offered to Fedorov, including deputy prime minister for military innovation, but the 35-year-old has said he would only return as defence minister.

A former minister of digital transformation, Fedorov set up a volunteer "IT Army of Ukraine" to launch cyber-attacks against Russians in the early days after its full-scale invasion.

Later, he led a successful fundraising campaign called the Army of Drones and brought in elements of "gamification" to the war, designing a system that awarded Ukrainian military units with credits for hitting Russian targets.

Ukraine's ousted defence minister has published a dramatic address demanding an election.

Mykhailo Fedorov, who was dismissed from his post last month amid public outcry, said in a video posted to YouTube: "Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia.

"We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amidst a prolonged war."

The former minister, who was once a staunch ally of Volodymyr Zelensky, said corruption in Kyiv had been harming its war effort, and claimed his country had been seeing a "systemic crisis of governance".

He said: "The old system lives by its own rules too often. It protects itself. It is scared of change."

Mr Zelensky has repeatedly rejected the notion of holding elections during wartime, despite demands from Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, as well as some factions of Ukrainian society.

Protesters took to the streets of Kyiv after the sacking of Mykhailo Fedorov - Reuters

Mr Fedorov's address came hours after Mr Zelensky announced that he would formally nominate Maj Gen Yevhen Khmara, a former security service (SBU) official, to take over the defence ministry.

His comments amounted to one of the most significant challenges to the Ukrainian president since the start of the war.

The former defence minister's trust rating soared from 35 per cent to 65 per cent after he was ousted in July, surpassing that of Mr Zelensky. In a poll published by the Rating Group that month, 72 per cent of respondents said they opposed his dismissal.

Several military officials and ministry advisers stepped down in protest at the decision.

Mr Fedorov's six-month tenure as defence chief was marked by a push to modernise Ukraine's armed forces through technology and reform military procurement in an attempt to address corruption.

The decision to remove him was followed by countrywide protests, but demonstrators' demands later shifted to calling for the dismissal of Oleksandr Syrskyi, the controversial army commander-in-chief with whom Mr Fedorov had clashed.

Mr Zelensky ceded to the public outcry on July 21, dismissing the 60-year-old general, who had led the military since 2024, but he refused to reinstate his reforming ex-defence minister, replacing him in an interim capacity with Maj Gen Khmara.
